title: Homotopy Type Theory
subtitle: Types as spaces, proofs as programs, equality as paths: a first course with Python labs and a circle explorer
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to homotopy type theory: types and terms, dependent Pi and Sigma types, propositions as types, identity types and paths, higher paths and groupoids, homotopy levels, equivalences and univalence, higher inductive types such as the circle, the fundamental group of the circle, and cubical type theory with proof assistants. Python labs recompute counts, reduce path words and compute winding numbers; two small interactive apps let you explore loops on the circle and propositions as types.

chapters.title: Why types? The big idea of HoTT

maps.title: Homotopy type theory
links: Univalence | says | Equivalent types are equal

summary: Homotopy type theory, or HoTT, reads types as spaces, terms as points, and equalities as paths between points. A proof that two things are equal becomes a path you can walk, bend and compose.
It combines two old ideas: Martin-Lof type theory, a foundation for mathematics and programming, and homotopy theory, the study of shapes up to continuous deformation.
The result is a foundation where equal things really are interchangeable, which is exactly what mathematicians always wanted equality to mean.

glossary.def: A collection of terms, such as Nat or Bool. Every term belongs to exactly one type.
An element of a type, written a : A.
A basic claim, such as a : A (a is a term of type A) or a = b : A (definitionally equal).
In HoTT, an identification of two terms of the same type.
The axiom that equivalent types are equal.
The reading where a statement is a type and a proof is a term of it.

keyPoints: a : A means the term a has type A, like 3 : Nat.
Statements are types; proofs are terms.
Equal means connected by a path.
Paths can be reversed and composed, like loops on a map.
Univalence: equivalent types are equal.
HoTT gives a foundation that proof assistants can check.

items: ELI5. Every thing in type theory carries a name tag saying what kind of thing it is. The number 3 wears a tag that says Nat. Equal things are things you can walk between.

In ordinary set theory, a thing can belong to many sets, and equality is a yes-or-no fact outside the system. In type theory every thing has a type, born with it, like a passport. The number 3 is a Nat, and that is part of what it is.

We write a : A for 'a is a term of type A'. We write A -> B for functions from A to B, and A x B for pairs. A new idea comes with a type: Bool has two terms, true and false. Nat has zero and a successor operation, so 0, 1, 2 and so on.

A judgment is a basic assertion that the rules can check. 3 : Nat is a judgment, and so is 2 + 1 = 3 : Nat, which says the two sides compute to the same thing. Judgments are about computation. They are not things you prove inside the theory.

The surprise is that logic comes for free. A statement like 'A implies B' is read as the function type A -> B, and a proof of it is a function that turns proofs of A into proofs of B. This is the Curry-Howard idea, and the next chapters build it up.

Then comes the homotopy. Equality of two terms a and b of type A is itself a type, written a = b. A term of it is a path from a to b. Two paths can be equal too, by a path between paths. The tower of paths between paths gives each type a shape.

Vladimir Voevodsky noticed in the 2000s that this matches homotopy theory. The program, with Awodey, Warren, Coquand, Shulman and many others, produced the HoTT book in 2013. Its flagship idea, univalence, says equivalent types may be treated as equal.

chapters.title: Functions, pairs and dependent types

maps.title: Pi and Sigma
links: Function type | is | A to B
Pair type | is | A times B

summary: A dependent type is a family of types B(x) indexed by x : A. For each x you get a type, called the fibre over x.

A dependent function type, Pi over x : A of B(x), has functions that send each x to a term in its own fibre B(x). A dependent pair type, Sigma over x : A of B(x), holds pairs of a point x and a term in the fibre over x.
When B does not depend on x, Pi becomes the function type A -> B and Sigma becomes the product A x B. Counting terms of finite types shows the names: Pi multiplies, Sigma adds.

glossary.def: A family of types B(x), one for each term x of A.
The type of dependent functions; its size is a product of the fibre sizes.
The type of dependent pairs; its size is a sum of the fibre sizes.
The type B(x) sitting over a point x.
A type whose terms are types, written U.

keyPoints: Pi: for all. Sigma: there exists.
|Pi x:A. B(x)| = product of |B(x)|.
|Sigma x:A. B(x)| = sum of |B(x)|.
Non-dependent Pi is A -> B; non-dependent Sigma is A x B.
A universe U holds small types as terms.

items: ELI5. A school has students and classes. Pick a class for every student, or pick one student with one class. Those two ways of picking are the two big kinds of type.
Think of a school. For each student x there is a set B(x) of classes the student attends. This is a family indexed by students. That is exactly a dependent type.

A Pi type is a rule that picks one class for every student. A Sigma type is a single pair: one chosen student together with one of that student's classes. 'For all' goes with Pi, and 'there exists' goes with Sigma.

Count with finite types. If A has 3 students and every student has 2 classes, a rule that picks one class for each student has 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 choices. A single pair of student and class has 3 x 2 = 6 choices, which is a sum 2 + 2 + 2.

When every fibre is the same type B, the Pi type is the ordinary function type A -> B with |B| to the power |A| terms. The Sigma type is the product A x B. Dependence adds nothing new, so the usual types are special cases.

To talk about families of types we need types as terms. A universe U is a type whose terms are types. The family B : A -> U assigns each point a type. Writing U : U would cause paradoxes, so in practice there is a hierarchy U0, U1, U2 and so on.

chapters.title: Propositions as types: Curry-Howard
summary: Under the Curry-Howard correspondence, a logical formula is a type and a proof of it is a program of that type. Proving a theorem and writing a program are the same activity.
Implication is a function type, and is proved by a function. And is a pair type. Or is a sum type, with a left and a right case. False is the empty type, and not-A means A -> False.
Excluded middle and double negation elimination have no general proof in pure type theory. Statements that need them are not provable constructively.

glossary.def: The correspondence between proofs and programs, and between formulas and types.
Writing a function as a binder, lam x. body.
Using a function on an argument, f a.
The type with no terms; it stands for False.
Logic where a proof of 'exists' must produce a witness.

keyPoints: A -> B is both implication and function.
A x B is both 'and' and pair.
A + B is both 'or' and sum.
Empty type: false. Not A is A -> Empty.
Excluded middle is not provable in pure type theory.

items: ELI5. A proof is like a recipe. If you can write a recipe that turns the ingredients A into the dish B, you have proved A leads to B.
Take the formula A implies A. It is true for any statement A, and the proof is easy: assume A and say it again. As a program that is the identity function lam x. x, of type A -> A.

Now A implies (B implies A). Assume A, then assume B, and then answer A. As a program, lam x. lam y. x. This function takes two arguments and returns the first. The type of the program is the formula it proves.

A simple type checker is a proof checker. Given the term lam x : A. x, it finds the type A -> A by looking at how the variable x is used. If the term does not typecheck there is no proof. This is the same logic as in the lab for this chapter.

And is a pair. To prove A and B, give a proof of each. To use it, take out a half with fst or snd. Or is a tagged choice: inl a or inr b. To use a proof of A or B, you must handle both cases, like a case split in a program.

False has no proof, so it is the empty type. Not A is the function type A -> False. A proof of not A turns any proof of A into a contradiction. Classical logic adds the law A or not A, but a program of that type would have to decide A, which is impossible in general.

In Haskell the same ideas show up in everyday code. The function const :: a -> b -> a is the proof of A implies (B implies A), and the type Either a b is a disjunction. A program that compiles is a proof of its type, as long as it terminates and uses no undefined.

identity x = x

constFn :: a -> b -> a
constFn x _ = x

swapPair :: (a, b) -> (b, a)
swapPair (x, y) = (y, x)

chapters.title: Identity types and paths

maps.title: Identity types
links: Path induction | proves | By refl only

summary: For terms a, b : A, the identity type a = b holds the proofs that a and b are equal. In HoTT we call a term p : a = b a path from a to b.
The basic path is refl : a = a. The induction principle for paths, written J, says that to prove something about all paths it is enough to prove it for refl.
From this one rule come symmetry (reverse a path), transitivity (compose paths), ap (apply a function to a path) and transport (move a term along a path).

glossary.def: The type a = b of identifications between a and b.
The constant path refl_a : a = a.
The rule that lets you assume a path is refl when proving things about all paths.
Applying a function f to a path p : a = b to get ap f p : f a = f b.
Moving a term in a fibre B(a) along a path p : a = b to a term in B(b).

keyPoints: refl : a = a.
Reverse: p : a = b gives inverse p : b = a.
Compose: p : a = b and q : b = c give p . q : a = c.
ap f p : f a = f b.
transport B p : B(a) -> B(b).

items: ELI5. Two places are equal if you can walk from one to the other. Walking back and forth, or joining two walks, are just ways to build new walks.
A path from a to b is a way to get from a to b inside the type. The simplest path stays put: refl at a. Because every type has refl at every point, every point is connected to itself.

From refl we can build the rest. To reverse a path, just walk it backwards. To follow a path from a to b, then a path from b to c, join them end to start. Joined paths are written p . q. Reverse paths are written p inverse.

A function carries paths with it. If f : A -> B and p is a path from a to a prime in A, then ap f p is a path from f a to f a prime in B. Functions respect equality, so 'equal inputs give equal outputs' is just ap.

Transport is the dependent version. A type family B over A tells you what sits over each point. If p is a path from a to b, then transport along p turns a term in B(a) into a term in B(b). Facts about a can be moved to b along any identification.

Path induction is the elimination rule. To prove a statement about every path p from x to y for all x and y, it is enough to prove it for refl at each x. This one rule gives you inverse, composition, ap and transport, and it is why proofs of equality can be so short.

lesson.code:
-- Agda-style sketch
sym : {A : Type} {a b : A} -> a == b -> b == a
sym refl = refl

trans : {A : Type} {a b c : A} -> a == b -> b == c -> a == c
trans refl q = q

ap : {A B : Type} (f : A -> B) {a b : A} -> a == b -> f a == f b
ap f refl = refl

practice.intro: Paths are lists of points, for example [1, 2, 3] goes from 1 to 3. Write compose(p, q): if the last point of p equals the first point of q, return the joined path with the shared point kept once; otherwise return an empty list. Write the answer for q starting where p ends.

practice.title: Inverse and ap
practice.intro: Write invert_apply(p, f): reverse the path p, then apply the function table f (a dict mapping a string of the point to a new point, with points as ints) to every point. Use f[str(x)] for point x. Return the new list.
practice.hint: Walk the list from the end.
practice.solution:
def invert_apply(p, f):
    r = []
    i = len(p) - 1
    while i >= 0:
        r.append(f[str(p[i])])
        i = i - 1
    return r

chapters.title: Higher paths and the groupoid structure

maps.title: Higher paths
links: Composition | is | Associative up to path
Loop | is | A path to itself
Loop space | holds | Loops at a point

summary: Paths are terms of the identity type, so two paths p, q : a = b can themselves be compared by the type p = q. A term of that is a 2-path, a path between paths.
Composition of paths is associative, has refl as a unit, and has inverses, but only up to a higher path. A type with this structure is an infinity-groupoid.
A loop at a is a path a = a. The loops at a form the loop space, and its structure is where homotopy groups come from.

glossary.def: A path between two paths with the same ends.
A structure with objects, reversible arrows, composition and identities.
A path from a point to itself.
The type of loops a = a at a base point a, written Omega(A, a).
Two compatible products on a set that share a unit must agree and be commutative.

keyPoints: p = q is a type; its terms are 2-paths.
Associativity: (p . q) . r = p . (q . r) by a path.
p . inverse p = refl by a path.
Loops at a form the loop space Omega(A, a).
Each type is a tower of paths: an infinity-groupoid.

items: ELI5. Two walks between the same places can sometimes be bent into each other. That bend is a path between paths, and you can keep doing this forever.

Take a map of a city with one-way and two-way streets. A path is a route. Two routes with the same ends are different, but you can ask whether one can be smoothly bent into the other. If so, there is a 2-path between them.

The laws of composition hold up to such bends. Joining three routes in one order or the other gives routes that are not identical, but they are connected by a bend. Going out and back along the same route can be shrunk to staying put, up to a bend.

There is no end to the tower, since 2-paths are also compared, giving 3-paths, and so on. A type with all these layers is an infinity-groupoid. This is how type theory sees a space: as points, paths, paths between paths, forever.

A loop at a base point a is a path from a to a. The loops at a form the loop space. Composition of loops gives a group-like structure. Taking loops again, loops of loops, gives the higher loop spaces, and those are commutative by the Eckmann-Hilton argument.

In the lab you work with the simplest model: free groupoid words. A route is a word in letters a and b, with capital letters for walking backwards. A letter followed by its inverse cancels. Reducing a word gives its normal form, the shortest route that is equal to it.

chapters.title: Homotopy levels: propositions and sets

maps.title: Homotopy levels
links: Proposition | has | At most one proof

summary: Types come in levels by how complicated their paths are. A contractible type is a single point up to paths. A proposition has at most one term up to paths. A set has no interesting paths between paths.
Level n + 1 means that all path types a = b have level n. The levels start at -2 for contractible, -1 for propositions, 0 for sets and 1 for groupoid-like types.
Truncation squeezes a type into a lower level. For example, a set truncation keeps only which component you are in, forgetting the paths.

glossary.def: A type with a center point such that every point equals it; level -2.
A type any two of whose terms are equal; level -1.
A type whose path types are propositions; level 0.
A type whose path types are (n-1)-types.
Turning a type into the closest type at a lower level.

keyPoints: Level -2: contractible. Level -1: proposition. Level 0: set.
A proposition has at most one proof.
A set has paths that are all unique.
Nat and Bool are sets.
Truncation forgets higher paths.

items: ELI5. Some shapes are a dot, some are a few dots, and some have holes. Counting how complicated their paths are gives them a level.

Look at a type from a distance. If it is just one point with nothing to wiggle, it is contractible, like a single dot. If it has at most one point, so any two proofs are the same, it is a proposition. These behave like true or false in ordinary logic.

If it has many points but each pair is joined by at most one path, it is a set. The natural numbers are a set: 3 is 3 in one way only. Sets are what ordinary mathematics uses, and in HoTT they are a special case.

If the paths of a type can themselves differ, but the paths between paths are unique, the type is a 1-type, or a groupoid. A circle is the typical example. Its loops are counted by the integers, which is the first interesting homotopy.

The level of a type is a property, not a choice. Sigma and Pi types preserve levels. A function type into a proposition is a proposition. This is why logic with propositions works well in HoTT: the usual rules hold.

Truncation makes the right statement for 'there exists'. A plain Sigma type remembers which witness, but we often only want to know that one exists. Propositional truncation squashes the Sigma type to a proposition, so existence means no more than just that it exists.

chapters.title: Equivalences and univalence

maps.title: Univalence
links: Path in U | is | An equivalence

summary: An equivalence between types A and B is a function with an inverse up to paths, written A ~ B. For sets it is exactly a bijection.
Every path A = B in the universe gives an equivalence, by transport. The univalence axiom says that this map is itself an equivalence, so equivalences are the same as paths in the universe.
Therefore equivalent types are interchangeable: any property proved for A can be transported to B.

glossary.def: A function with a two-sided inverse up to homotopy.
A function between sets with an inverse; an equivalence of sets.
The map from paths A = B in a universe to equivalences A ~ B is an equivalence.
Moving structure or properties from one type to an equivalent one.
An invertible structure-preserving map; univalence makes isomorphic structures equal.

keyPoints: A ~ B: a function with an inverse up to paths.
For finite sets, equivalence = bijection.
Univalence: (A = B) is equivalent to (A ~ B).
Isomorphic things are equal; use either.
n points have n! self-equivalences.

items: ELI5. If two toys are the same in every way that matters, you can swap them. Univalence says the math may treat them as one and the same toy.

In everyday mathematics, we say two things are 'the same' if they are isomorphic, and then we freely replace one with the other. But set theory does not support this: a statement about one may be false for the other if it looks at the details of how it is built. Univalence fixes that.

An equivalence is a function f with an inverse g such that going there and back is homotopic to doing nothing. For two sets, this is simply a bijection. For richer types there is extra data, because the homotopies must be coherent.

Take any path between two types in the universe. Transport along the path gives an equivalence, so every identification yields one. The axiom says the reverse: every equivalence arises, uniquely, from a path. So A = B and A ~ B are the same.

The consequences are strong. Anything you prove about a type, like a group structure, can be carried over to an equivalent type automatically, with no special proof. The principle that isomorphic structures are indistinguishable becomes a theorem.

Count to see equivalence at work. A set with 3 points has 3! = 6 self-equivalences, the permutations. The type of equivalences from a 3-point set to itself has exactly six points, and the path space of the 3-point set in the universe also has six points. They match, as univalence predicts.

chapters.title: Higher inductive types: the circle
summary: An ordinary inductive type lists point constructors. A higher inductive type, or HIT, may also list path constructors: new equalities that must hold.
The circle S1 has one point base and one path loop : base = base. The interval has two points and a path joining them. Spheres and other shapes are built the same way.
These are the types that let HoTT reason about real shapes directly.

glossary.def: A type defined by point constructors and path constructors.
The HIT with a point base and a loop base = base.
The HIT with points 0, 1 and a path between them; it is contractible.
The HIT with two poles and a path from north to south for every point of the original type.
To map out of a HIT, say where each constructor goes.

keyPoints: S1: base : S1 and loop : base = base.
Interval: two ends joined by a path; it is contractible.
Suspension of S^n is S^(n+1).
To map out of S1, give a point and a loop in the target.
HITs add shape, not just data.

items: ELI5. A circle is a dot with a rope tied back to itself. Going around once is different from not moving, and going around twice is different again.

Imagine defining the natural numbers: zero, and successor. Now imagine a type with one point, and one path from that point back to itself. That is the circle. It has base, a point, and loop, an identification of base with itself that is not equal to refl.

The loop is not trivial, and that is the whole point. A path that goes around once is different from standing still. Going around twice gives a different path again. The paths base = base look like the integers: loop to the n for any whole number n, with negative numbers meaning the other way.

To define a function out of the circle you must say where base goes and what loop goes to. A point in the target and a loop at that point are enough. This is the recursion principle, and for the circle it means that maps S1 to X are the same as loops in X.

The interval has two points, zero and one, and a path between them. It looks like a line, and it is contractible. Because it has a path from zero to one, it gives a way to prove that equal functions are equal by a path, which is function extensionality.

The suspension of a type A has a north pole and a south pole, and for every point of A a path from north to south. The suspension of two points is a circle, and the suspension of a circle is a two-sphere. Spheres of every dimension come out by repeating it.

chapters.title: Homotopy groups and the fundamental group of the circle

maps.title: Homotopy groups
links: pi1 of circle | is | The integers
Freudenthal | stabilizes | pi k of spheres

summary: The n-th homotopy group of a pointed type is the set of n-fold loops, with 'same up to a path' as equality. For n = 1 this is the fundamental group.
The fundamental group of the circle is the integers. In HoTT the proof uses a type family over the circle, whose fibre over every point is the integers and where transport along loop adds one.
The homotopy groups of spheres are a famous hard table. Some entries are easy, and some are still being computed.

glossary.def: The group of loops at a base point up to paths; pi1(A, a).
pi_n(A, a), the n-fold loops at a, with truncation to a set.
Prove a path space is some type by building maps in both directions using transport.
A type family over the circle with fibre Z, used to prove pi1(S1) = Z.
Suspension eventually becomes an equivalence on low homotopy groups.

keyPoints: pi1(S1) = Z: loops are counted by integers.
Encode: send a loop to its winding number.
Decode: send n to loop to the n.
pi_k(S^n) = 0 for k < n; pi_n(S^n) = Z.
Stable groups appear by Freudenthal.

items: ELI5. Wind a rope around a pole. The only thing that matters is how many times and in which direction, so loops are counted by whole numbers.

Use a rope and a pole. A loop of rope around the pole can be undone only by unwinding it. How many times it winds around, and in which direction, is an integer. This count is what the fundamental group of the circle measures.

To prove the group of loops at base in S1 is Z in HoTT, first define a family of types over the circle. Its fibre at every point is Z, but going around the loop shifts the integers by one. So transport along loop is adding one.

Then encode: transport the integer 0 along a given path to get an integer, which counts the winding. Decode: for n, go around the loop n times. The two maps cancel. This is called the encode-decode method, and it is how most path spaces are computed in HoTT.

Higher homotopy groups come from loops of loops. The circle has none: pi_k of S1 is trivial for k above 1. The two-sphere is different. It has pi_2 = Z, and also pi_3 = Z, a famous surprise from the Hopf fibration.

Spheres have a table that grows ever more complex, with finite groups like Z/2 and Z/12 scattered in it. The Freudenthal theorem says that after enough suspensions the groups stop changing, which gives the stable homotopy groups. HoTT proves such theorems in the same language as everything else.

chapters.title: Cubical type theory and proof assistants
summary: Plain HoTT assumes univalence as an axiom, so programs using it can get stuck. Cubical type theory builds paths from an interval, so univalence computes.
Cubical Agda is a proof assistant with these features. Rocq (formerly Coq) has HoTT libraries, and Lean has a large library of ordinary mathematics.
The HoTT book, free online, is the standard introduction. This course is a gentle path to it.

glossary.def: A version of type theory where paths are functions from an interval, and univalence has computational meaning.
A variant of Agda with cubical features.
Software that checks formal proofs written as typed terms.
Functions that agree at every point are equal; provable via the interval.
Homotopy Type Theory: Univalent Foundations of Mathematics, 2013.

keyPoints: Cubical: a path is a function from the interval.
Univalence computes in cubical type theory.
Agda, Rocq and Lean can all check proofs.
The HoTT book is free and written by a large group.
Types you write in Haskell show the idea in small.

items: ELI5. Computers can check a proof as if it were a program. Some tools even let the paths run like code, so the proof can actually compute.

The axiom of univalence is added from outside to plain type theory. That is fine for a proof, but a program built with it cannot always run, because the axiom has no computation rule. This bothers people who like programs that evaluate.

Cubical type theory makes paths concrete. A path from a to b is a function from an interval, taking a at one end and b at the other. With this, composition, transport and univalence all compute. It also gives function extensionality for free.

To try this yourself, use a proof assistant. Cubical Agda has the new features built in. Rocq has a HoTT library and Lean has a very large collection of mathematics, though with different foundations. You give each one terms, and it checks the types.

Haskell cannot state dependent types fully, but it can show the main ideas. A GADT can index a type by a value, a type class can carry evidence, and phantom types can mark facts at compile time. These give a feel for how types carry proofs.

Where to go next? Read the first chapters of the HoTT book, then try path induction and the circle in a proof assistant. Compute pi1(S1) once yourself. After that the rest of the book, about higher inductive types, cohomology and the cumulative hierarchy, is open to you.

lesson.code:
-- Haskell: a vector indexed by its length (a dependent-type taste)
{-# LANGUAGE GADTs, DataKinds, KindSignatures #-}
data Nat = Z | S Nat

data Vec (n :: Nat) a where
  Nil  :: Vec 'Z a
  Cons :: a -> Vec n a -> Vec ('S n) a

-- head only accepts a nonempty vector, checked by the type
vhead :: Vec ('S n) a -> a
vhead (Cons x _) = x
